connection: Session 30 used constructor injection to replace a repository during tests. Session 30B now studies the runtime container that constructs services and controls instance reuse.
objectives: Identify the composition root as the place that chooses implementations and lifetimes.
Predict and observe transient, scoped, and singleton identity within and across scopes.
Explain why lifetime selection matters when objects hold mutable state.

visuals.title: The composition root is the assembly bench
visuals.explanation: Registrations gather in one deliberate place where the application chooses which concrete types satisfy requests and how long their instances live.

visuals.title: Transient creates a fresh ticket every time
visuals.explanation: Two resolutions, even inside one scope, return two different TransientMarker objects.

visuals.title: Scoped shares one tray per scope
visuals.explanation: Repeated resolutions inside the first scope reuse one ScopedMarker, while the second scope receives a different instance.

visuals.title: Singleton is one lighthouse for all scopes
visuals.explanation: Both scopes resolve the same SingletonMarker instance from the provider. Shared mutable state would therefore be shared across all consumers.

preQuiz.prompt: Where should an application normally choose implementations and lifetimes?
preQuiz.explanation: The composition root centralizes object-graph decisions.

preQuiz.prompt: What should two transient resolutions return?
options: The same instance in one scope
preQuiz.explanation: Transient creates a new instance for each resolution.

preQuiz.prompt: Which lifetime reuses one instance inside a scope but not across scopes?
preQuiz.explanation: Each scope owns one scoped instance.

concept.title: Constructor injection and a container are related but different
paragraphs: Session 30 passed a repository directly into ClockEntryService. That is constructor injection and does not require a container.

A DI container stores construction rules and builds object graphs. IServiceCollection holds registrations; BuildServiceProvider creates the resolver. The composition root is the application location that owns those choices.
concept.code:
ServiceCollection services = new();
using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider();

concept.title: Registration chooses one reuse rule
paragraphs: The marker types in this experiment are intentionally empty. Holding behavior constant leaves object identity as the only evidence: blank marker; visible identity.

services is the registration collection. AddTransient, AddScoped, and AddSingleton select the reuse rule; the generic type argument names the registered service; parentheses invoke the registration method.

concept.title: Predict identity before resolving
paragraphs: ReferenceEquals answers whether two variables point to the same object. The intellectual work is predicting that answer from the resolution boundary, not repeatedly typing similar declarations.
Use the anchors: transient—new every request; scoped—one per scope; singleton—one per provider.

concept.title: Refresh the generic Resolve helper
paragraphs: Read the signature from left to right. private limits use to this experiment; static means the method uses its parameter rather than LifetimeExperiments instance state; the first T is the return type; Resolve<T> declares the method type parameter; IServiceScope scope is the ordinary parameter; where T : notnull disallows a nullable requested service type.
For Resolve<TransientMarker>(firstScope), every T becomes TransientMarker. GetRequiredService<T>() returns the registered non-null service or throws when the registration is missing.

concept.title: Disposal follows type information and ownership
paragraphs: Hover a type or use Go to Definition to look for IDisposable or IAsyncDisposable. Documentation may also state whether the caller owns the returned object, and the compiler rejects using for an incompatible type.

ServiceProvider owns its scopes and container-created disposable services. Because this experiment creates the provider and scopes, it owns their disposal. Using declarations dispose in reverse declaration order: second scope, first scope, then provider. Use the anchor: I created it, it is disposable, so I probably own its disposal—unless the API says otherwise.

lab.title: Observe Three DI Lifetimes
lab.objective: Register, resolve, and compare transient, scoped, and singleton instances in two explicit scopes.
lab.task: Print four identity comparisons whose true and false results prove each lifetime rule.
lab.startingCondition: Session 30 completed isolated service tests. The learner ScratchPad has no Session30B experiment and does not yet reference Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.

steps.text: Setup code — choose either workflow to add Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection version 10.0.0 to the ScratchPad project. The CLI command updates the project file and restores the package; manual PackageReference editing remains a valid alternative.

In the ScratchPad project, create folder Session30B and file Session30B/LifetimeExperiments.cs. Add using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, declare public sealed class LifetimeExperiments, and add an empty public void Run method.

Before writing registrations, add three private sealed nested classes inside LifetimeExperiments but outside Run: TransientMarker, ScopedMarker, and SingletonMarker. Give each an empty body. No namespace is missing; these nested types are visible throughout their containing class. Memory anchor: Blank marker; visible identity.
Build the ScratchPad project in Release so the marker declarations compile before any registration references them.

Learning code — inside Run, create ServiceCollection services. Study the three registration forms shown, then type them. Read each as: use this collection, choose this reuse rule, register this marker type, and invoke the method.
steps.purposeAfter: The marker types now exist and the collection contains three construction rules, but no marker object has been created yet. Resolution begins only after the provider and scope boundaries exist.

steps.text: Setup code — paste the provider and two scope declarations shown. ServiceProvider, firstScope, and secondScope are disposable owners created by this method, so using declarations give them deterministic cleanup. Hover or use Go to Definition to find IDisposable; the compiler also rejects using for an incompatible type. Cleanup occurs in reverse declaration order: secondScope, firstScope, then provider.
steps.purposeAfter: The provider can now apply the registrations, and two distinct scope boundaries exist. The next work resolves marker objects through those boundaries; the container—not the registration calls—creates them.

steps.text: Retrieval refresher — inside the class but outside Run, type private static T Resolve<T>(IServiceScope scope) where T : notnull. Read it left to right: private access, static helper, T return type, T method type parameter, ordinary scope parameter, then a non-null type constraint. Return scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<T>(), which returns a registered non-null service or throws when registration is missing.

Learning code — before resolving anything, copy this prediction table into a temporary comment or notes area and fill every blank with true or false. Explain each choice with: transient—new every request; scoped—one per scope; singleton—one per provider.

steps.text: Learning code — write the first complete comparison yourself. Resolve TransientMarker twice from firstScope into firstTransient and secondTransient. Display Transient reused in one scope with ReferenceEquals for those variables.

Learning code with setup scaffolding — use the partial resolution block shown for the remaining comparisons. Replace each blank with firstScope or secondScope according to the prediction table. Do not retype unchanged scaffolding merely for repetition.
Setup code — paste the three repeated display statements shown. Before continuing, confirm that each ReferenceEquals pair tests one row of your prediction table.
Review the four comparisons before integration. For each one, point to the registration rule, the first resolution boundary, the second resolution boundary, and your predicted Boolean.
steps.purposeAfter: The experiment now contains one fully authored transient pattern and three targeted variations. It needs a caller only so ScratchPad can display the identity evidence; Program.cs does not teach another lifetime rule.

steps.text: Setup code — in ScratchPad Program.cs after earlier session calls, print a Session 30B heading, create LifetimeExperiments, and call Run. Preserve all earlier experiments. Run ScratchPad once, then reconcile every observed Boolean with the prediction table.
steps.purposeAfter: The focused run should show false, true, false, true and prove all three reuse rules. Final validation has a different job: confirming that the new package and permanent experiment did not damage the cumulative solution.

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: The complete experiment gives each lifetime its own named resolution and predicted identity result.

lab.expectedBehavior:
Transient reused in one scope: False
Scoped reused in one scope: True
Scoped reused across scopes: False
Singleton reused across scopes: True
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

review: The experiment stays in permanent ScratchPad rather than changing production registrations.
Each lifetime has a separate named identity comparison and predicted result.
The provider and both scopes are deterministically disposed.
No mocks, repositories, EF Core, HTTP, or async work is introduced.

options: To distinguish reuse within a scope from reuse across scopes
postQuiz.explanation: Scoped identity changes only when the scope boundary changes.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can singleton mutable state be risky?
options: All consumers share the same instance
postQuiz.explanation: One shared instance means shared mutations and concurrency responsibilities.

options: No, callers can construct and pass dependencies directly
postQuiz.explanation: A container automates construction; constructor injection itself is a class design.

reflections: Which code is the composition root of this experiment?
Why does scoped require two separate comparisons?
When would shared singleton state be intentional, and what safeguards would it need?
whatBreaks: Removing the second scope makes across-scope behavior impossible to observe. Replacing named resolutions with one compressed expression hides which instance belongs to which boundary. Omitting disposal loses explicit ownership of provider-created resources.
summary: A DI container applies construction and lifetime rules chosen at a composition root. Transient creates per resolution, scoped reuses within one scope, and singleton reuses across scopes owned by one provider. ReferenceEquals makes those ownership rules visible.
